rows.en: As we have seen in the question of the laying on of hands, so it is with all the enactments of the elders and with all the decrees that the sages of the generations decreed in those days: they were forced upon them by the time and by the events. For they never invented decrees, enactments and fences out of their own heart, to load them on people, if there was no need for them. And if for most of them the reason has been lost and we have only conjectures about them, this is only because afflictions and hardships without number have been a darkness between us and the earlier generations. From Yose ben Yoezer and Yosef ben Yoḥanan two decrees have also remained, which came in the wake of the time and the events. They decreed impurity on the land of the nations, and they decreed impurity on glass vessels (Shabbat 46b⚠1, and the Yerushalmi there). The decree of impurity on the land of the nations was without doubt due to their wish to put a check on the dispersion of the people in the lands of the gentiles. For because of the persecutions with which they were persecuted by the government, and through the troubles that came in the wake of the persecutions, many left their native land and went to live in the lands of the nations, to find a resting place for the sole of their foot. Therefore, to restrain the people from scattering in the land of the gentiles, they decreed impurity on the land of the nations, knowing⚠2 how many drew back because of impurity; and the masters of the Talmud have already testified to this (Yerushalmi Yoma 2:1, and the Bavli there), that impurity was harder for them than bloodshed. And perhaps they also had in this a hidden intention against the Ḥasidim, who at a later time were called by the name Essenes. For the first who rose up in war against Antiochus were the Ḥasidim, but not all of them had the strength to stand by their purpose; rather, many of the Ḥasidim drew back from the war and escaped for their lives to hide in the wilderness, and perhaps also escaped to foreign soil. This was evil in the eyes of the sages and the Ḥasidim who were in Jerusalem, and therefore they decreed impurity on the land of the nations, to check their dispersion. The second decree, by which they decreed impurity on glass vessels, was without doubt decreed because of new knowledge that had reached them about the making of glass and its material: it became known to them that its nature is close to that of earthenware, and therefore they treated it in several respects like earthenware and decreed impurity on it (Kelim ch. 2). From Yose ben Yoezer in particular three things are handed down concerning laws. But it was not he who invented them; rather, he held them as received from earlier Scribes, and he testified to them. He testified: "that the ayil kamtza [a kind of locust] is clean; that the liquids of the slaughterhouse [of the Temple] are clean; and that one who touches a corpse (is masav, or) mistaav [becomes impure]" (Eduyot 5:4; Sifra Shemini; Pesaḥim 15a; Avodah Zarah 37b). These halakhot are remarkable of their kind, in that they are handed down in the Aramaic language, which is not the case with any one of all the ancient halakhot; and we learn from this that this tradition is old. Without doubt the people of his generation were strict in these matters until Yose came and permitted them, and because of this they called him "Yose the Permitter." It is further clear from this that when he says dikrav be-mita mistaav, the stress is not on mistaav, as if he wanted to teach that one who touches a corpse becomes impure; for there would be no need of his testimony and his tradition for that, since it is written so in the Torah, nor would he deserve on that account to be called "Yose the Permitter," for he would have permitted nothing. Rather, the stress is on dikrav, and he means to say: only one who touches with certainty and knows that he touched shall be impure, but not one who is in doubt whether perhaps he became impure. And this halakhah was necessary for them at that time, when, since impurity was grave in their eyes, many without doubt held back from going out to war for fear of impurity, lest⚠3 they become impure through the slain of the sword. Therefore he ruled for the need of his hour that only one who certainly touches becomes impure, and against certain impurity one can guard oneself; but in a doubtful touch there is no impurity.{v1_06_12:1}

2.note: Printed so; read as a misprint for מדעתם ('knowing', 'from their knowledge'), since מרעתם gives no sense.

3.note: אן as printed; read as a misprint for אם/פן, 'lest'.

rows.en: A moral saying of Yose ben Yoezer has also remained to us: "Let your house be a meeting place for the sages, and dust yourself in the dust of their feet, and drink their words with thirst" (Avot 1:4). How very fitting these words are to the events of his time, when the chief effort of the government and of its friends and flatterers among the sinning Jews was to keep the people far from the religion and from the Torah and to stop study and inquiry, until they were forced to do their deeds in the dark and to hide from the violence of the oppressor (2 Maccabees 14:5). All the books of the Torah or other holy writings that were found they condemned to burning or destruction, and whoever had them found with him, there was one law for him: to be put to death (Josephus 12:5). For this reason Yose roused the hearts of the good among the people to open their houses to be a meeting place for the sages, and not to let their hands go from the Torah, and to drink with thirst its words and the words of its teachers. From Yosef ben Yoḥanan too sayings have remained to us which also bear the marks of his time: "Let your house be open wide, and let the poor be members of your household, and do not talk much with the woman" (this too there). How precious these words are for his time and his generation, when many were pressed and forced to transgress their religion and for this reason became poor and needy; and so he warned them that each should help his fellow and strengthen his arms. And in particular there is in this a mark of the character of the sect of the Ḥasidim (the Essenes), who came out of the first Ḥasidim of that time. When we see that this Ḥasid widens the measure of the kindness that a man shows to his fellow so far as to make it a statute and a duty that his house be open wide and that the poor be counted as members of the household, is not the distance from a degree of kindness such as this to the custom of association in the manner that came about among the Essenes in the course of time no more than one step? That is, that all who entered the covenant of their society should have one law with the members of the society in their money and in all their possessions. So too the saying "do not talk much with the woman" was also a rule for the Essenes, except that they went with it to the furthest extreme and held back from association with women altogether, until most of them did not take wives. Yose ben Yoezer was called "the pious one of the priesthood" (Ḥagigah, end of ch. 2). And they said of him that his kerchief was midras [impure as a thing trodden on] for holy things. This sheds light on the character of his piety: for although he was the pious one of the priesthood, nevertheless he did not cross the bound of piety to sanctify and purify himself beyond measure, but guarded himself from impurity with the care proper for those who eat terumah, and no more. When these two sages died, the eshkolot ceased (Sotah 9:9). These were heads under whose hand were all the affairs of the people in all branches of office, and they were called ish kol ["a man of everything"] (Rav in the Bavli there). And it is rightly said that they ceased, for in the time of the Hasmoneans and after them, under the rulers of the house of Herod, the power of the sages diminished, and it was no longer as in former days.{v1_06_13:1} Of the life of Yosef ben Yoḥanan nothing has reached us beyond what has been told so far; of his origins and his death we know nothing. But the death of Yose ben Yoezer was evil and bitter, and his last words have remained to us, and they bear witness to the character of his spirit and the strength of his power in his faith. The high priest Yakim (Alcimus), the traitor to his people, was of his family (according to the account of the midrash, his sister's son), and this sinner denied even his own kin so as to carry out the evil he had planned to do. When he came with his schemes to the people, saying, "Peace shall be yours from the government!", they trusted him, saying, "Is he not of the seed of the priests? He will do us no harm and will not deceive the sons of his people." But their trust was false; for what he spoke to them with the smoothness of his tongue he did not fulfill. He laid his hand on sixty of the Ḥasidim, and by his command they were all killed (1 Maccabees 6:14–15⚠1). Even on Yosef⚠2 ben Yoezer, his kinsman, he had no pity, and he condemned him to death. And when this Ḥasid was led to be crucified, Yakim tried once more to turn him from his mind, and said to him: "See all the good and the honor that have come to me because of my ways and my deeds, and against this the great evil that has brought you to die like one of the base, for your stiff neck." But Yose answered him with calm of soul: "If it is so for those who anger God, how much more for those who do His will!" And Yakim said to him: "And who did His will more than you?" And Yose answered him: "If it is so for those who do His will, how much more for those who anger Him!" Words like these, from the mouth of a man as exemplary and pious as Yose, would break even a heart hard as rock; and indeed they did not miss their mark. For these last words of his went down into the chambers of the high priest's belly and came like murder into his bones, and he killed himself (Genesis Rabbah 65). But others told of him that he died a sudden death (the book of Maccabees and Josephus). And although the whole story is wrapped in the mantle of aggadah, nevertheless we can hold as clear truth that Yose ben Yoezer had a kinsman of his family who was called Yakim; that this Yakim is none other than Alcimus, who was high priest at that time; and that Yose was one of those killed for the sanctification of the Name who were killed at the command of Alcimus. The masters of the Talmud further mention that Yose ben Yoezer had a son who did not behave properly, and his father put him out of his inheritance and consecrated all that he had to Heaven. The son went his own way and married into [the family of] one of the servants of Jonathan the Hasmonean, and he grew very rich, for he found a precious pearl of great value and sold it to the treasurers who were over the Temple treasury. But the value of the pearl was thirteen aliyot (the name of a small vessel; see the *Arukh*) of gold denarii, and in the Temple treasury there were only seven aliyot. He took the seven that were there and left the rest of the price to the sanctuary as a gift. They stood up and wrote: "Yose ben Yoezer brought in one (referring to the property he consecrated) and his son took out seven" (Bava Batra 133a). Now it is not our purpose to investigate the basis and the root of this aggadah;{v1_06_14:1} only this much can we hold: that Yose ben Yoezer had a son who also was enticed to walk in a way that was not good, like many of the people of his generation, until his father removed him from his inheritance. And who knows whether the basis of this aggadah is not one with what is told, that Yose had a sister's son, namely Alcimus, who did not behave properly, and the two, the son and the sister's son, are one, and he is Alcimus and none other (R. A. Geiger, *Urschrift*, p. 64 and on). Besides all this we have nothing of the life of these sages. Nor do we have any matter or saying on which their names are recorded, except the sayings and the matters that we have mentioned. But when we see how careful they were to urge the people to make their houses a meeting place for the sages and to support inquiry, and also to inquire and to gain understanding with all their strength, we can judge from this that with all the hardships and troubles that befell them at that time they did not cease to inquire in the Torah; and without doubt many matters that are mentioned without the names of those who said them should be attributed to these two sages and to the sages of their time. And it is also for this reason that the generations that came after them praised them and said that from the days of Moses until their time there was no blemish in all the eshkolot that arose for Israel (Temurah 15b; Tosefta Bava Kamma ch. 8). And one of the later sages said that from the days of Moses until Yose ben Yoezer died they learned Torah like Moses our teacher, and from then on they did not learn Torah like Moses our teacher (Temurah there). The meaning is plain: until that time there were no disputes, and from their time on the disputes began, especially the disputes of the Sadducees against the Pharisees, because forgetfulness was growing. For even if it is clear that under the pressure of the troubles they did not cease to hold fast to the Torah, nevertheless it is not possible that in the days of the troubles that now came upon them some traditions were not forgotten.

1.note: Printed so, with no closing parenthesis; the sixty Ḥasidim killed by Alcimus are in 1 Maccabees 7:12–16.

2.note: Printed יוסף; the story is about Yose ben Yoezer.

rows.en: Yose ben Yoezer fell before the sons of wickedness; Yosef ben Yoḥanan also died and was no more. The days of wrath and trouble that now came upon Israel held them back in their walking on the path of the Torah. The good among the people and those who cleaved to the Torah were weary of bearing any longer the pressure with which they were pressed by the government to turn them from their religion. A few men of the Ḥasidim rose up out of the zeal for the Lord of hosts that was within them, with Mattathias son of Yoḥanan the priest at their head, and they stood against a great army of the king's force and, leaning on the Lord, prevailed. Judah Maccabee his son did great valor and fought the wars of the Lord, and he prospered in all his wars. Judah fell on the heights of the field of slaughter. Jonathan his brother filled his place, and he too showed great valor; but he fell by guile into the hands of an enemy who brought him down to death. Then Simon his brother became head in his stead, and he completed the freedom of Israel. A time of upheaval such as this was not suited to increasing studies and enlarging the Torah. We do not know who the heads of the Torah were at that time, but we know of one office without the names of its holders and heads, namely the court of the Hasmoneans. In the days of Jonathan's rule there was a great court in Jerusalem; for when Jonathan sent a letter of peace to the people of the Lacedaemonians to renew the covenant between them and the Jews, the great council stood at the head of the signatories. So too, when Simon was appointed to be prince, the elders and the heads of the people are also mentioned (Josephus, *Antiquities* 13:5; 1 Maccabees 14:27). Now these heads were without doubt the court of the Hasmoneans, from whom some statutes and ordinances in matters of the Torah have been handed down to us, but they are few. The events from the beginning of the coming of the Greeks into their land had made them know that nothing harms the religion of the Jews more than association with the gentiles who are around them or who live among them. This association gave birth to the sect of the sinners who changed the holy religion and walked in the ways of the Greeks, and it turned many of Israel from the way of the Torah, to turn their hearts away from the Lord, the God of their fathers. Therefore they readily recognized that their first duty was to create a distance between themselves and the nations of the land. We have already seen that in the days of Yose ben Yoezer they decreed impurity on the land of the nations. All the more so, after they had attained their freedom and the rod of wickedness was broken, they strove greatly to keep far from them. For this reason too they decreed in the court of the Hasmoneans against any intimacy of the flesh between an Israelite and a foreign woman, with a stringency beyond what the Torah forbade (Avodah Zarah 36b). And certainly, because of this keeping apart, they found occasion to decree on other matters as well, especially in matters of impurity, for the keeping of purity was in their eyes like an iron wall between them and the nations of the land; but the decrees are not recorded under their name, for most of the decrees of the early sages are recorded anonymously, and the names of those who decreed them sank into oblivion. They further made an enactment to celebrate every year a festival of eight days in memory of the miracles that were done for them, and it was called Ḥanukkah, because first and foremost it was made for the dedication [ḥanukkat] of the altar. It runs from the twenty-fifth day of the month of Kislev onward for eight days. They established on it the kindling of lights, a light for each man and his household, and the celebration of this festival with hallel and thanksgiving to the name of the Lord (Shabbat 21b). This hallel is what had already been fixed at an early time to be said in the Temple in memory of the miracles and the salvation that were done for them (above, ch. 8, in the note), and it is called hallel because it begins with halleluyah and ends with halleluyah. And then, after Judah Maccabee had defeated his enemies and they had cleared the Temple that the Greeks had defiled, one of the poets of the time composed a psalm to give thanks to the Lord; it begins with hodu ["give thanks"] and ends with hodu, and therefore it is called hoda'ah ["thanksgiving"] (Psalm 118). In it is mentioned that the nations surrounded them to destroy them and to thrust them down, and the Lord helped them; they give thanks that God did not give them over to death, and that they came as of old to His sanctuary, and its gates were opened to them.{v1_06_15:1} This thanksgiving they established to be said on Ḥanukkah, and they attached it to the hallel that had already been fixed of old. These enactments without doubt went out from the court of the Hasmoneans. One more thing is told of them: that by their word the altar stones that the Greeks had defiled as abominations were stored away (Middot 1:6). They could not decide on their impurity, so they took a vote on them and stored them away (see *Megillat Ta'anit* ch. 8; Yoma 15⚠1; Avodah Zarah 52b) until Elijah comes and testifies concerning them (1 Maccabees 4:44–46). And all this is from the court of the Hasmoneans.{v1_06_15:2}

1.note: Printed so, without a side of the leaf; the passage is at Yoma 16a.

rows.en: Besides the court of the Hasmoneans, the writers of the chronicles mention other, different names by which they call the sages of the Torah of that time, namely: Ḥasidim (the book of Maccabees, in many places) and elders (Josephus, *Antiquities* 12). The Ḥasidim were the first who were zealous with the zeal of the Lord of hosts and the zeal of His Torah, and they fought with all might and strength. In the course of the days of the war many drew back for fear, because they could not keep the religion and the commandments of the Torah properly according to their view. Little by little they went out of the measured character of piety into excess, and in the measure of their piety they went to the furthest extreme. They lived a life of hardship in solitude and spent their time in searching out the hidden. They took up customs that differed from the customs of the true Ḥasidim, their companions or their originals, from whom they had come out. Now these true Ḥasidim and the elders of this period are mostly mentioned by the names "the first Ḥasidim" and "the first elders." We have from them remnants and precious sayings. The remnants from the Ḥasidim include matters of their customs and their deeds, and the remnants from the elders are various matters in the midrash of the Torah and halakhah, and also words of moral instruction (*Darkhei ha-Mishnah*, p. 40). They said of the first Ḥasidim that they used to wait one hour and then pray, so that they might direct their hearts to their Father in heaven; and even if the king greeted them, and even if a snake was coiled around their heel, they did not interrupt (Berakhot 5:1); and they paid no heed to danger to life where a commandment was concerned.{v1_06_16:1} We see from this the degree of their piety: in every matter touching the keeping of the commandments of the Torah they stood ready to give their lives for it. Yet we are told of them in another place (Shabbat 121b) that the spirit of the Ḥasidim was not pleased with one who kills snakes and scorpions on the Sabbath. And although the title "the first" is not mentioned there, nevertheless, from what is made clear there of how careful they were in keeping the Sabbath, it appears that this refers to the first Ḥasidim, or at any rate to those who walked in their ways. Now with men for whom the keeping of the Sabbath weighed more than danger to life, it does not surprise us that they refrained from fighting on the Sabbath even when the danger was near, as happened in the days of Mattathias, when many of them were killed and did not stand up for their lives for fear of profaning the Sabbath; until afterward, when Mattathias saw that this was not the way to attain the aim of their desire, they took a vote and decided to fight and to stand up for their lives even on the Sabbath day. And if we want to know how far their piety reached with respect to the Sabbath, let us see what is told of them in the Talmud (Niddah 38a): the first Ḥasidim took care not to approach their wives on the fourth day [of the week], for if she conceived on that day, the days of her pregnancy would be completed, according to their view, on the Sabbath, and if she went into labor they would be forced to profane the Sabbath for her; and for this reason they refrained from approaching her on the fourth day. Therefore we rightly judge that the Ḥasidim whose spirit was not pleased with one who kills snakes and scorpions on the Sabbath are the very Ḥasidim known by the title "the first." And without doubt they were likewise strict in the other commandments of the Torah. We also find an excess by which they went beyond the commandments of the Torah in the commandment of tzitzit too (Menaḥot 40b). Toward people as well they conducted themselves by the measure of piety, and it is told of them that at all times they took care that no harm should come about through them. Therefore it was their way to hide thorns and broken glass in the midst of their fields, digging three handbreadths deep into the earth for them, so that the plow would not bring them up and people stumble on them (Bava Kamma 30a, and the Yerushalmi there 3:3).

footnotes.en: In *Darkhei ha-Mishnah*, p. 32, he explains this halakhah: the people of Yose's generation wanted to be stringent with one who touches a corpse, a "father of fathers" of impurity, [treating him] like the corpse itself, so that he would be masav (for in his view the source of impurity, such as a corpse, a zav, etc., is called masav); and on this Yose testified dikrav be-mita mistaav, that is, mistaav but not masav (in his view mistaav indicates a lower degree than masav), for he is at a lower degree than the masav, that is, the corpse, and becomes only a "father" of impurity. Thus far his words. But this needs proof that the reading "mistaav" is the original one; for in the Gemara the reading is masav, and so was the reading in the Mishnah before Maimonides, and R. Obadiah of Bertinoro followed him, and so is the reading of the Tosafot in Nazir (42a). And even if it were so, the explanation in itself is open to doubt. For his intention is evidently that the Ḥasidim wanted to decree that one who touches one who touched should be impure like one who touches the corpse itself, and Yose came and testified that it is not so: one who touches a corpse is not masav but mistaav, that is, he is not like the corpse itself, and therefore one who touches one who touched is not like one who touches a corpse. But these are exactly the words of the Gemara, which says: "They decreed dikrav be-dikrav," that is, one who touches one who touched shall be impure like one who touches a corpse, that is, with seven-day impurity; "and he came and said: dikrav is impure, but dikrav be-dikrav is not impure" with seven-day impurity, except when they are joined. And Rava in the Gemara refuted this explanation. Therefore I have withdrawn my hand and taken hold of the explanation of Rav Naḥman, which Rava brought in his name. One should also remark on the incident that R. Judah told there, that Yose ben Yoezer set up beams for them and said: "Up to here is the public domain, up to here the private domain." We cannot decide that this incident has any relation to the halakhah of Yose, but this much is clear: that this incident prompted Rav Naḥman to his explanation.

See the book *Urschrift* of R. A. Geiger, p. 116 and on, who wrote that the word eshkol is compounded of ish kol, as Rav said in the Bavli, and that it is the exact translation of the Greek word katholikos; and if so, it is right to call the leaders of the community, who are appointed over all matters of administration, eshkolot. And this is what they said in Yerushalmi Shekalim 5:3: "There were two katholikin." This is the first office after the Nasi and the high priest. But what he wrote there, that they are the Pairs, still needs proof; for before Yose no Pairs are mentioned, and after him there were no leaders for all matters, but only in matters of religion and Torah. In a baraita in Yerushalmi Sotah it is taught: "All the Pairs who arose from the death of Moses until Yose ben Yoezer arose, one can find fault in them; until Judah ben Bava arose, one can find fault in them." And on this the rabbi relied [to say] that eshkolot are the same as Pairs. But the baraita is corrupt from beginning to end and truncated, and one cannot rely on it. The main reading is as it is in Tosefta Bava Kamma ch. 8, and there they read "all the eshkolot," and they also read "one cannot find fault in them"; but the Tosefta too is corrupt, in that it reads "from the death of Yose" etc., and what was [said] "from the death" is missing there, and one must correct it according to the Yerushalmi, that is: "from the death of Yose one can find fault in them." Thus from the one and from the other the correct reading is supported, and so without doubt was the reading before the Bavli (Temurah 15b). And see vol. 3⚠1, ch. 4, p. 34, what I conjectured on the explanation of the word eshkolot.

1.note: ח"ג read as 'vol. 3'; the work meant (Weiss's own or another) is not stated.

footnotes.en: See in the book *Urschrift* of R. A. Geiger what he wrote on this aggadah. And see in the Gemara of Bava Batra that I cited; there it says that he married the daughter of the crown-weaver of King Yannai; and in my opinion this Yannai is Jonathan son of Mattathias.

The whole of Psalm 118 fits very well the time of the victory of the Maccabees. And the baraita that says "in the following year they fixed them and made them festival days with hallel and thanksgiving" refers to the two parts of the hallel: the first part begins and ends with halleluyah, and the second part is the one that begins and ends with hodu. This baraita is very old, and whoever composed the praise that is said on Ḥanukkah, "In the days of Mattathias" etc., already had the baraita before his eyes, for there it says: "and they established these eight days of Ḥanukkah to give thanks and to praise Your great name." This corresponds to the words of the baraita, "they fixed them and made them festival days with hallel and thanksgiving." But the wording of the baraita is more exact: first hallel and afterwards thanksgiving, in the order of the two parts of the hallel. The composer of this prayer was not exact in this, and perhaps he did not understand that the baraita said "with hallel and thanksgiving" deliberately, to hint at the two parts of the hallel.

See Graetz, vol. 3, at the end of the book, p. 485, who corrected well the reading in *Megillat Ta'anit*. And one should remark that in Middot the reading is "the sons of the Hasmoneans," and in Yoma and Avodah Zarah the reading is "the house of the Hasmoneans"; perhaps one should read "the court of the Hasmoneans," and the expression "they took a vote on them and stored them away" indicates this too.
